staged_description.title: Housing Discrimination Lawsuit
staged_description.description_short: In 1973, the Justice Department sued Donald Trump, Fred Trump and their company over alleged racial discrimination in rental housing. The 1975 consent decree barred…
staged_description.description_medium: The Justice Department sued Donald Trump, Fred Trump and Trump Management in 1973, alleging Fair Housing Act violations. The complaint described Black applicants being denied vacancy information or steered elsewhere. The case ended in a 1975 consent decree barring discrimination and requiring training, equal-housing ads and vacancy lists for the New York Urban League. The decree expressly did not admit liability.
staged_description.description_long: The Justice Department filed suit in October 1973 in the Eastern District of New York against Donald Trump, his father Fred Trump, and Trump Management, alleging violations of the Fair Housing Act across 39 buildings containing more than 14,000 apartments. The Civil Rights Litigation Clearinghouse case file says the complaint relied in part on paired testing: white testers were told about vacancies while Black testers were not or were steered to different properties. It also alleged employees used codes beside applicants’ names to indicate race. The defendants counterclaimed for defamation; the court dismissed that counterclaim and allowed the federal case to proceed. The parties resolved the case through a consent decree signed June 10, 1975. It barred discrimination in rental terms and practices, required Donald and Fred Trump to familiarize themselves with the Act, and required advertisements stating that minorities had equal opportunity to apply. Trump Management also had to provide the New York Urban League weekly vacancy lists for two years. The decree expressly stated that it was not an admission of a violation. The record supports the filing, allegations, and negotiated obligations, but not a claim that a court found the defendants liable.
